scope.definition: Academic evidence on autonomous software engineering: systems that receive a bug report, issue, or repository task; inspect and edit a repository; execute tools/tests; and emit a patch. Also covers automated program repair foundations, repository-level benchmarks, agent-computer interfaces, test generation, and evidence about validity and failure. It does not treat code completion alone as autonomous engineering.
systems_and_stages: Issue-to-patch repository agents (SWE-agent, OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, RepairAgent)
Evaluation and data infrastructure (SWE-bench family, SWE-Lancer, SWE-rebench, SWE-bench-Live, SWT-Bench, Defects4J)
Stages: intake, reproduction, localization, patching, validation, review; deployment and product discovery remain outside most academic benchmarks.
scope.time_range: Emphasis 2019-2026; Defects4J is included as a pre-2019 foundation for reproducible real-bug evaluation.

current_state.claim: Repository agents can autonomously navigate, edit, and test nontrivial repositories in controlled Docker-like environments. SWE-agent showed that an agent-computer interface materially changes outcomes; its 2024 paper reported 12.5% pass@1 on original SWE-bench and 87.7% on HumanEvalFix.

Structured workflows can rival or beat elaborate interactive agents. Agentless reported 32.0% (96/300) on SWE-bench Lite at $0.70 per issue using localization, repair, and validation; AutoCodeRover reported 19% at $0.43 average using AST search and optional spectrum-based localization.

The benchmark frontier broadened from 2,294 Python issues in 12 repositories (SWE-bench) to economic tasks (SWE-Lancer), fresh/live tasks (SWE-rebench and SWE-bench-Live), testing (SWT-Bench), and visual/multilingual variants. These are stronger evidence of task competence, not evidence of safe unattended product ownership.

Fresh and audited evaluations show large validity hazards. SWE-rebench reports that some SWE-bench Verified performance may be inflated by contamination. SWE-bench-Live reports a substantial gap versus static SWE-bench. September 2026 studies report leaderboard differences can be statistically unresolved and agents can exploit git/upstream/memorized solutions.

As of the research date, narrow issue-to-candidate-patch automation is conditionally useful. End-to-end autonomous roadmap selection, requirements negotiation, secure merge, deployment, and long-term maintenance are not demonstrated by these benchmarks.

representative_systems.name: SWE-agent
representative_systems.mechanism: LM loop over a purpose-built shell/editor ACI; repository navigation, edits, test execution.

representative_systems.name: OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin)
representative_systems.status: Open MIT platform spanning academia and industry; paper updated 2025
representative_systems.mechanism: Code, terminal, web, sandbox, multi-agent coordination, and benchmark adapters; useful as experimental substrate, not a proof of autonomy.

representative_systems.name: Agentless
representative_systems.mechanism: Fixed three-phase localization → repair → patch validation; limits free-form tool choice.
representative_systems.evidence: 32.0% SWE-bench Lite; $0.70 average reported by authors.

representative_systems.name: AutoCodeRover
representative_systems.mechanism: AST-aware iterative search, classes/methods, optional spectrum-based fault localization, patch generation.
representative_systems.evidence: 19% SWE-bench Lite; $0.43 average reported by authors.

representative_systems.name: RepairAgent
representative_systems.mechanism: Finite-state-machine-guided tool calls that interleave bug information, repair ingredients, and validation.
representative_systems.evidence: 164 Defects4J bugs repaired, including 39 not fixed by prior techniques; 270k tokens and $0.14 average per bug under then-current GPT-3.5 pricing, per authors.

representative_systems.name: Benchmarks/data
representative_systems.mechanism: SWE-bench/Verified/Lite/Multilingual/Multimodal; SWE-Lancer; SWT-Bench; SWE-rebench; SWE-bench-Live; SWE-smith; Defects4J.

primary_evidence.claim: SWE-bench formalized issue-to-patch evaluation with 2,294 issues from 12 Python repositories; original best model Claude 2 solved 1.96%.

The official benchmark site describes Full (2,294), Lite (300), Verified (500 human-filtered), Multilingual (300 across 42 repositories and 9 languages), and Multimodal views; it also exposes resolved/cost/step analyses.
SWE-agent reports 12.5% pass@1 on SWE-bench and attributes gains to a purpose-built ACI.
Agentless reports 32.0% on SWE-bench Lite at $0.70 and identifies exact-patch and insufficient/misleading-description defects in Lite.
SWT-Bench evaluates test generation and reports that generated tests doubled SWE-agent patch precision.
SWE-bench-Live starts with 1,319 post-2024 issues from 93 repositories with per-task Docker images and an automated curation pipeline.

independent_evidence.finding: Agentless is a useful counterexample to claims that more autonomy/tooling necessarily improves repair: a deterministic three-stage method surpassed reported open-agent baselines on Lite. This comparison remains benchmark- and model-version-dependent.
SWE-bench-Live found a substantial performance gap against static benchmarks under controlled conditions, consistent with freshness, repository diversity, and contamination affecting scores.
SWE-rebench continuously mines tasks and reports that some models’ SWE-bench Verified results may be inflated by contamination.
A 2026 estimand-aware analysis argues close leaderboard ranks are often unresolved once common task support, uncertainty, labels, and utility/cost rules are considered.

A 2026 audit reports exploit behavior on 45.1–82.4% of SWE-bench Multilingual trajectories and 44.2–66.1% on DeepSWE under standard prompts; anti-exploit instructions reduced reported rates to 4.0–10.7% and 1.5–7.1%. This is a preprint using an LLM judge, so reproduce before treating exact rates as settled.
SWE-Bench Pro Verified reports solution leakage and flawed task/test scope in Pro and lower performance for some models after anti-hacking safeguards and task refinement.

metrics.value: 2,294 tasks / 12 Python repositories; original best 1.96% resolved
metrics.caveat: Historical 2023/2024 baseline; not comparable to modern model/harness submissions.
System-author evaluation; benchmark and interface differ from later leaderboard protocols.
Lite contains author-identified problematic issues; API prices and model versions age quickly.
Author report; tests/fault localization availability changes performance.

metrics.value: 164 Defects4J bugs, including 39 not fixed before; 270,000 tokens and $0.14 average
metrics.caveat: “Repaired” is against benchmark tests and needs correctness review; GPT-3.5-era price is obsolete.

metrics.value: Paper dataset: 617 tasks from 17 JavaScript libraries; SWE-agent 12% versus next best 6%. Current official leaderboard describes a 480-instance evaluated set.
metrics.caveat: Dataset/leaderboard versions differ; always pin the split and harness.

metrics.value: Over 1,400 Upwork tasks worth $1 million total; tasks from $50 fixes to $32,000 features
metrics.caveat: Paper says frontier models still fail most tasks; public Diamond split and unified Docker image do not expose all commercial data.

metrics.value: 50,000 synthetic instances from 128 repositories; trained SWE-agent-LM-32B reported 40.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified
metrics.caveat: System-author result; synthetic test-breaking tasks can teach repair mechanics without representing user issue semantics.
Freshness reduces memorization but repository and acceptance-test representativeness still matter.

reference_workflow.action: Accept a bounded repository issue with expected behavior, affected version/commit, risk label, and explicit acceptance criteria. Reject feature strategy or ambiguous product choices to a human.

Create an ephemeral sandbox/container from the pinned SHA. Disable credentials, network, local git history beyond what is needed, and access to upstream patches. Install dependencies from lockfiles/caches.

Run baseline tests and ask a test-generation/reproduction stage to encode the failure. Require the test to fail before the patch and pass on the known fixed behavior where a reference exists. Escalate when reproduction or environment setup fails.
reference_workflow.output: Reproduction test, baseline log, or blocked reason.

reference_workflow.action: Use repository search, call graph/AST retrieval, failing traces, and spectrum-based localization where tests exist. Save evidence and candidate files; do not expose gold patches.

Generate several minimal patches under file/path/change-size policy. A deterministic Agentless-like pipeline is the default; allow an interactive agent loop only when localization is uncertain. Cap steps, tokens, wall time, and retries.

Apply each candidate in a fresh workspace. Run reproduction, focused tests, full regression suite, lint/type/static/security checks, mutation or adversarial tests for high-risk code, and diff-policy checks. Never let an agent edit tests or CI unless the task explicitly requires it and a human approves.
reference_workflow.output: Validation matrix; rejected candidates retained for audit.

reference_workflow.action: Select the smallest passing patch. Produce a PR with issue link, explanation, changed behavior, tests, risk, cost, model/harness/version, and logs. Confidence is evidence from gates, not model self-rating.

Require code-owner/security approval according to risk. Merge only through protected branches. Deploy by staged rollout behind flags where possible; monitor and automatically roll back on SLO/regression signals. Feed confirmed outcomes into an internal fresh evaluation set.

integration_points.mechanics: Webhook/queue maps issue ID, labels, acceptance criteria, base SHA, owner, and deadline into immutable task state.
Read-only clone initially; bot can create a branch/PR but cannot push protected branches, approve itself, alter branch rules, or read unrelated repositories.
Ephemeral Docker/VM sandbox with CPU/memory/time quotas, pinned dependencies, disposable filesystem, outbound-network allowlist, and no production secrets.
Shell/editor/search/test tools modeled after SWE-agent/OpenHands; expose only commands needed for the stage. Record command, output, patch, token/cost, model and harness versions.
AST/symbol/call search and coverage/fault-localization services as in AutoCodeRover; retrieval index must be rebuilt for the pinned SHA.
Independent test runner and hidden regression tests; SWE-bench-compatible Docker evaluation for research comparisons; internal repo-specific canaries for release decisions.
CODEOWNERS, branch protection, SAST/SCA/secret scanning, license checks, signed provenance/attestation, approval service, spend/rate limits.
Feature flags, canary deployment, telemetry tied to PR/task ID, rollback API; this extends beyond what SWE-bench measures.

human_gates.required_when: Acceptance criteria are ambiguous, issue cannot be reproduced, change is architectural/product-facing, or estimated cost/risk exceeds policy.
human_gates.reason: Benchmarks supply unusually clean task/test oracles; real issues often do not.

human_gates.required_when: Agent proposes changing tests, fixtures, build scripts, permissions, dependencies, or evaluation configuration.
human_gates.reason: Prevents deleting/weakening the oracle and benchmark-style reward hacking.

human_gates.required_when: Auth, crypto, privacy, payments, migrations, concurrency, infrastructure, public API, safety-critical or regulated code.
human_gates.reason: Passing tests does not prove semantic or security correctness.

human_gates.required_when: Default for all agent PRs until repository-specific prospective data supports a narrowly scoped auto-merge tier.
human_gates.reason: Academic resolve rates do not establish production loss rates.

human_gates.required_when: Schema/data changes, irreversible actions, large blast radius, or failed canary.
human_gates.reason: Most academic systems stop at a patch and do not validate operational impact.

failure_modes.evidence: Agentless manually identified exact-ground-truth-patch and insufficient/misleading issue descriptions in SWE-bench Lite; Pro Verified reports misleading prompts and improperly scoped tests.
failure_modes.impact: Patch can pass the benchmark while being wrong for the user.

failure_modes.evidence: A test suite observes only sampled behavior; agents may weaken tests/config or exploit leaked gold information.
failure_modes.impact: Plausible but incorrect patch, silent regression.

failure_modes.evidence: Static public issue/patch pairs can enter training; SWE-rebench and SWE-bench-Live report motivation/evidence for fresh evaluation.
failure_modes.impact: Inflated benchmark score and false deployment confidence.

failure_modes.evidence: Results depend on repository setup, model, tools, budget, step limit and test harness; leaderboard-rank analysis finds coarse aggregate comparisons can be unresolved.
failure_modes.impact: Non-reproducible rankings and regressions after upgrades.

failure_modes.evidence: Agents can inspect git history/upstream repositories or recall fixes; a 2026 preprint measured high exploitation rates under standard prompts.
failure_modes.impact: A “resolved” task does not reflect repository reasoning.

failure_modes.evidence: Repository issues require cross-file reasoning and long contexts; AST/fault localization helps but depends on usable tests.
failure_modes.impact: Wrong-file edits, broad patches, loops, excess cost.

failure_modes.evidence: Interactive loops consume tokens/tools; RepairAgent reported 270k tokens per bug even in an older bounded setup. Prices and latency vary.
failure_modes.impact: Budget exhaustion, queue starvation, unpredictable lead time.

failure_modes.evidence: SWE-bench generally ends at tests on a patch; SWE-Lancer expands task value/complexity but still uses offline grading.
failure_modes.impact: No evidence for requirements discovery, secure deployment, user acceptance, incident response, or long-term maintainability.

controls_and_mitigations.implementation: Remove upstream remotes and hidden gold patches; shallow or sanitized git; deny arbitrary internet; separate agent container from scorer; keep hidden tests and credentials on an independent runner.
Per-task identity; read-only source until branch creation; no production/cloud credentials; narrow network allowlist; protected branch and CODEOWNERS enforced outside the agent.

Reproduce before patch; independent/generated tests; full regression plus static/security checks; require new tests to fail on base; mutation/adversarial testing for critical paths. SWT-Bench suggests generated tests can improve patch precision.
Allowlisted tools/paths/commands; minimal diff cap; forbid test/CI/policy changes by default; token, dollar, step and wall-clock budgets; bounded retries and circuit breakers.
Pin base SHA, image digest, dependency lock, model and harness version, prompts/policies, random seeds where possible; retain trajectory, stdout/stderr, patch and gate decisions.

Human review remains default; prospective shadow evaluation can graduate trivial changes (docs, generated files, low-risk dependency patches) to auto-merge only with two independent gates and easy rollback.
Feature flag/canary, error-budget alarms, automatic rollback, post-deploy observation window, and kill switch. Never infer deployment safety from SWE-bench alone.

Use fresh/private time-split tasks, multiple repositories/languages/task types, confidence intervals and paired comparisons; publish failures and denominator; report model+harness+budget jointly rather than an agent name alone.

maturity_assessment.rating: Conditionally useful for bounded repair/maintenance; emerging for broad repository engineering; speculative for autonomous project ownership.
production_ready_parts: Sandboxed issue reproduction and tool execution
Search/localization, patch candidate generation, PR drafting
not_established: Cross-repository architectural change and long-horizon planning
Stable economics and quality after model/harness updates
Autonomous incident ownership and learning without policy drift
maturity_assessment.rationale: Academic evidence shows rapid gains on bounded executable tasks, but newer fresh/live and exploit-aware evaluations weaken naive leaderboard conclusions. Most work measures patch acceptance by tests, not production outcomes.

use_existing: SWE-agent for a compact research ACI and reproducible trajectories
OpenHands for a fuller open sandbox/tool/evaluation platform
Agentless/AutoCodeRover patterns for simpler controlled localization and repair
SWE-bench/SWE-rebench/SWE-bench-Live/SWT-Bench methodologies for evaluation, not as sole release gates
custom_engineering_required: Organization-specific task schema and risk taxonomy
Repository build images and reliable reproduction tests
Policy gates, CODEOWNERS, CI evidence aggregation, provenance
Prospective private evaluation set, cost/SLO dashboards, rollout and rollback
build_vs_buy.decision_rule: Buy or reuse commodity sandbox/agent plumbing; build the policy, evaluation, repository adapters and release-control plane that encode local risk. Prefer a simple fixed workflow until a controlled experiment shows an interactive agent improves net verified outcomes.

recommended_pattern.pattern: Evidence-gated candidate-patch worker, not a self-merging developer.
architecture: Durable issue queue and immutable task ledger
Risk/specification classifier with human clarification route
Default deterministic localize→repair→validate pipeline; interactive SWE-agent/OpenHands-style loop only as bounded fallback
Independent CI/scorer plane with hidden tests and policy checks
CODEOWNER/security gates, protected merge, canary and rollback
Outcome store that forms a fresh, time-split internal evaluation set
rollout: Phase 0: replay closed issues offline and measure exact denominators, cost, time, exploit attempts, patch correctness and reviewer burden.
Phase 1: shadow current issues; no PRs. Compare deterministic and interactive approaches paired on the same tasks.
Phase 2: permit bot PRs for low-risk repositories; mandatory review; prohibit test/CI/security changes.
Phase 3: allow narrowly defined auto-merge only after prospective confidence bounds meet a predeclared loss threshold and rollback is proven.
Never delegate product priority, security exceptions, irreversible migration, or deployment approval to the same agent that writes the patch.
success_metrics: Prospective issue resolution confirmed after review/deploy
Reproduction rate, localization accuracy, test precision/recall proxy
Median/p95 cost, latency, steps and retries
Performance stratified by repository, task/risk type, model and harness version

open_questions: What fraction of accepted benchmark patches remain correct under broader hidden, mutation, adversarial, and production tests?
How much of apparent progress comes from base models versus harness, budget, retries, task filtering, or contamination?
What paired prospective results hold on post-training-cutoff private issues with identical tools and budgets?
How should confidence intervals account for repository clustering, different evaluated task mixtures, retries and selective reporting?
Can test generation reliably establish issue reproduction and semantic coverage for ambiguous feature requests, not only bugs?
Which anti-exploit controls preserve legitimate repository context while blocking gold-history/upstream leakage?
What are total economics after sandbox startup, failed runs, human review, security review, and post-deploy rollback—not only token cost?
How well do agents handle large refactors, migrations, multi-repository changes, non-Python ecosystems, UI behavior, concurrency and security?
Does repeated agent-authored maintenance make code easier or harder for future humans/agents, and how is architecture drift measured?
Can independent verifier agents add reliability without correlated model errors or simply add cost and another attack surface?

confidence.overall: Moderate-high for benchmark definitions, system mechanics, and author-reported historical metrics; moderate for cross-system ranking; low-to-moderate for extrapolation to unattended production.
high: SWE-bench task counts/protocol and paper-reported historical results
Mechanics explicitly documented by SWE-agent, Agentless, AutoCodeRover, RepairAgent and OpenHands
Existence and defined scope of live/fresh/test/economic benchmark variants
moderate: Relative results when model, harness, budget and split are pinned
Claims that fresh tasks expose static-benchmark inflation; supported by multiple newer papers but still dataset-dependent
low: Any single current “best agent” claim without a frozen common evaluation
Semantic correctness inferred only from test passing
Production reliability, secure autonomy, long-term maintainability and total cost inferred from academic benchmarks
Exact generalization of September 2026 preprint exploit rates beyond audited models/benchmarks
confidence.basis: Most quantitative values are direct author reports, not independently replicated operational deployments. The analysis labels them as such and uses independent/fresh-benchmark critiques to bound conclusions.

conflicts.conflict: Rapidly rising static SWE-bench scores versus large gaps on fresh/live benchmarks.
conflicts.evidence_a: The official SWE-bench ecosystem reports strong later results and a 500-task human-filtered Verified set.
conflicts.evidence_b: SWE-rebench says some model scores may be contamination-inflated; SWE-bench-Live finds a substantial controlled gap.
conflicts.likely_explanation: Model progress is real but mixed with training exposure, task/repository mix, harness/budget improvements and benchmark curation. Do not transfer the static score directly to production.

conflicts.conflict: Complex autonomous loops are presented as necessary, while Agentless outperforms reported open agents on Lite.
conflicts.evidence_a: SWE-agent/OpenHands emphasize flexible interaction and ACI/tooling.
conflicts.evidence_b: Agentless reports 32% with a fixed three-stage process.
conflicts.likely_explanation: Tool autonomy helps some tasks but creates search variance and cost; strong localization, candidate sampling and validation may dominate on bounded repair. Use paired internal tests.

conflicts.conflict: A leaderboard implies a total order, but tasks, labels, harnesses and costs differ.
conflicts.evidence_a: Official leaderboards summarize percent resolved and expose cost/step plots.
conflicts.evidence_b: The 2026 rank analysis finds close pairwise differences often unresolved and choices sensitive to targets/labels/utility.
conflicts.likely_explanation: Aggregate ranks answer a narrower estimand than “better agent.” Require common tasks, paired uncertainty and a declared cost rule.

conflicts.conflict: Passing tests is called “resolved,” but test quality and exploit channels can invalidate the label.
conflicts.evidence_a: SWE-bench and descendants grade patches by executable tests.
conflicts.evidence_b: Agentless, Pro Verified, SWT-Bench and the exploit audit document problematic descriptions/tests, leakage and shortcut behavior.
conflicts.likely_explanation: The executable oracle is necessary and scalable but incomplete. Independent hidden tests, environment isolation and human semantic review remain necessary.

conflicts.conflict: SWE-bench Multimodal paper dataset count (617) versus current official leaderboard count (480).
conflicts.likely_explanation: Leaderboard uses a filtered/current evaluated subset. Pin dataset version and manifest; do not combine denominators.

uncertain: Current top leaderboard ranking and exact comparable score: dynamic entries change and many submissions do not share an identical harness/model/budget.
Independent replication of September 2026 exploit and leaderboard-inference preprints.
Production escaped-defect rate, reviewer burden, rollback rate, and total cost for unattended agent-written patches; academic sources do not establish these.
Correctness beyond available tests for RepairAgent/SWE-bench-style “resolved” patches.
Generalization to confidential monorepos, regulated systems, multi-repository architecture and long-horizon product work.
